subject: geography
title: Park's Response Curve
welcome_lead: Trace community recovery through three phases.
meta_desc: A-Level Geography adventure on Park's hazard response curve and disaster timelines.
final_note: Recovery trajectory depends on aid, governance and capital.

concepts.def: Three-phase response curve: relief, rehabilitation, reconstruction.
Immediate (hours-days) emergency response: search-rescue, medical aid.
Weeks-months: restore services, temporary housing, plan recovery.
Months-years: rebuild infrastructure better than before.
Reconstruction stronger and more resilient than pre-disaster state.
Plots quality of life vs time from pre-event baseline through dip and recovery.

walkthroughs.body_html: Park's curve plots quality of life vs time. Pre-event baseline drops sharply during impact. Relief (hours-days) stabilises decline. Rehabilitation (weeks-months) restores function. Reconstruction (months-years) ideally exceeds pre-event level.

Mw 9.0 quake and tsunami killed 18500, displaced 470000. Relief mobilised within 24 hours; SDF deployed 100000 personnel. Reconstruction budget ~£200 billion. By 2021, most areas exceeded pre-disaster quality of life through seawalls and infrastructure.

Limited governance, weak infrastructure and slow international coordination stalled the curve. 1.5 million displaced; cholera outbreak (introduced by UN troops) killed 10000 more. Pre-event quality of life not reached even a decade later.

mcqs.q: What is lag time on a storm hydrograph?
options: The three cells are tropical, temperate and arctic, named after climate zones.
Lag time is the delay between thunder and lightning.
The time between peak rainfall and peak river discharge — affected by drainage basin shape, land use, soil saturation and vegetation.
Lag time is how long the storm itself lasts.

mcqs.q: What are the three cells of global atmospheric circulation?
options: Lag time is the delay between thunder and lightning.
The Hadley cell (equator to 30 degrees), Ferrel cell (30 to 60 degrees) and Polar cell (60 degrees to poles) together redistribute heat from equator to poles.
The three cells are tropical, temperate and arctic, named after climate zones.
There is one big Hadley cell from the equator to each pole.
